extracted.intended_audience: Readers of The Spectator; literate early-18th-century general public
extracted.subtask_description: Short, public moral and social essays (Spectator-style) offering prescriptive commentary on authorship, civic virtue (planting), and personal morals (dreams/self-examination). The page models periodical-essay norms and moral advice for a general reading audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed works should convey truth and knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is a melancholy thing to consider, that the Art of Printing, which might be the greatest Blessing to Mankind, should prove detrimental to us, and that it should be made use of to scatter Prejudice and Ignorance through a People, instead of conveying to them Truth and Knowledge.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues the fundamental duty of print and writers is to communicate truth and knowledge to the public; printing used to spread prejudice/ignorance is a misuse. (Context: contrasts illuminating vs. tenebrificous authors.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Be an illuminating author, not a 'tenebrificous' one
rubrics_metrics.description: From the William Ramsey quotation and commentary: "Some of them are Stars that scatter Light as others do Darkness. I could mention several Authors who are tenebrificous Stars of the first Magnitude... The Nation has been a great while benighted with several of these Antiluminaries.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should aim to 'scatter light'—to enlighten readers—rather than produce darkening, obscure, or misleading works. The essayist threatens to 'drive them quite out of the British Hemisphere.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the pathology of the perpetual periodical writer
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of periodical writers: "there is no Species of Scriblers more offensive, and more incurable, than your Periodical Writers, whose Works return upon the Publick on certain Days and at stated Times... One Day makes Work for another, we do not know when to promise our selves Rest.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodic publication should not be an endless, self-perpetuating exercise that tires readers; value is placed on works that have completion or do not endlessly churn out trivial copy. Remedies (satyrs, lampoons, pillory, cat-calls, or forbidding pen/ink/paper) are mentioned satirically as punishments for the worst offenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers should aim for concision and an achievable 'end'
rubrics_metrics.description: Implied by lament that with periodical writers "our Progress... is never at an End. One Day makes Work for another" and the Diogenes anecdote about taking comfort in reaching the end of a dull book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good writing gives readers the consolation of eventual completion; periodical composition should respect readers' time by avoiding interminable prolixity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planting as a virtuous, public-minded employment
rubrics_metrics.description: "Among these I know none more delightful in itself, and beneficial to the Publick, than that of PLANTING... I do not only recommend this Art to Men of Estates as a pleasing Amusement, but as it is a kind of Virtuous Employment... particularly from the Love which we ought to have for our Country, and the Regard which we ought to bear to our Posterity.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planting is presented as a moral duty and civic virtue for landowners: it beautifies the country, benefits posterity (timber for fleets), and is appropriate even for men of high rank. The essay offers both aesthetic and moral rationales for encouraging planting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small, inexpensive acts (planting twigs) produce long-term public benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: "When a Man considers that the putting a few Twigs into the Ground, is doing good to one who will make his appearance in the World about Fifty Years hence... he is perhaps making one of his own Descendants easy or rich, by so inconsiderable an Expence...",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages evaluation of civic actions by long-term impact; even modest, low-cost efforts (planting a few twigs) are praised as effective contributions to posterity and evidence of generous character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer durable, improving labours (like planting) over ephemeral works
rubrics_metrics.description: "Plantations have one Advantage in them which is not to be found in most other Works... when you have finished your Plantations, they are still arriving at greater Degrees of Perfection as long as you live... When you have finished a Building... it immediately decays..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects that continue to improve over time (e.g., planting) are morally and aesthetically preferable to undertakings that peak and decay; this is offered as a standard for evaluating the worth of occupations and investments of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily self-examination (use dreams and waking imagination to judge character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice modelled on Pythagoras: "That every Night before they slept they should examine what they had been a doing that Day... If I might second the Philosopher's Advice, it should be mine, That in a Morning before my Scholar rose, he should consider what he had been about that Night...",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical prescription: examine your waking and nocturnal imaginations to discover what actions and vices to pursue or prevent. Go to bed with a mind free from passion and a body free of intemperance to ensure salutary dreams and useful introspection. Uses examples of rehearsing business in sleep to gain advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purify yourself before judging others
rubrics_metrics.description: From the vision account: the instructor says, in effect, that "before you can be qualified to see and animadvert on the Failings of others, you must be pure your self." The dream-procedure involved cutting out and squeezing the writer's heart to reveal hidden faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral critics should undertake self-purification and honest introspection before censuring others; the essay uses the phantasmic heart/phial imagery to illustrate attending to one's own vanity, envy, greed, etc., as prerequisites for fair critique.
